title: Intellectual property, licensing, policy and accountability

items.scenario: Three weeks into a project, a developer finds a SOW clause: 'Supplier shall not use third-party AI services on Client materials without prior written consent.' The team has been using the organisation's enterprise Claude seats on client code.
items.question: What should happen next?
options: Carry on, because an enterprise plan's data terms already protect the client's material
Stop using Claude on the client's material, escalate to the lead and legal, and seek consent
Switch to personal accounts so the organisation's enterprise usage stays clean
Add a disclaimer to all future deliverables saying AI tools may have been used on this account
items.explanation: The client contract governs the relationship with the client. Provider terms can't override a clause that requires consent, so stop, escalate and get consent before resuming.
distractors: Provider terms govern you and the provider. They don't satisfy a client clause requiring written consent.
Personal accounts add a shadow-AI breach on top of the contract breach.
A disclaimer isn't consent. The clause requires prior written consent.

items.scenario: Claude suggests an AGPL-3.0 PDF library for a feature in your multi-tenant SaaS product. The code would run on your servers and never be distributed as a binary.
items.question: How should you treat the suggestion?
options: Accept it, because AGPL obligations only apply when you distribute compiled binaries to customers
Accept it if the library's README describes it as free and open source
Treat it as blocked pending licence review, and look for verified permissive alternatives
Accept it but remove the licence header from any copied files
items.explanation: AGPL treats offering the software over a network like distribution, so SaaS use can trigger source obligations. Copyleft goes through the approved-list review.
distractors: That's the GPL trigger. AGPL adds network interaction, which is exactly the SaaS case.
'Open source' says nothing about the obligations. The licence terms decide.
Stripping licence notices breaches even permissive licences and doesn't remove AGPL obligations.

items.scenario: A contractor admits they pasted client production logs into their personal Claude Pro account because their company seat was still being provisioned.
items.question: What is the right response?
options: Have them delete the chat today. Since nothing was trained on, no further action is needed at all
Treat it as a data incident: report it under the client contract, then fix the provisioning delay
Tell them it's fine as long as they upgrade the personal account to Max
Ask Claude in the same personal account to confirm the logs were not retained
items.explanation: Client data processed under consumer terms with no audit trail is a contract and data-handling problem. Handle it as an incident, then fix the root cause (provisioning lag) that pushed the person to shadow AI.
distractors: Deleting the chat hides the event. It doesn't undo the processing or meet notification duties.
A different consumer tier doesn't make it an approved, organisation-governed plan.
The model can't attest to retention. That's governed by terms and admin controls.

items.scenario: Your team wants an automation that compiles the weekly client status report from Jira with Claude and emails it to the client every Friday.
items.question: Where should the human approval gate go?
options: After the email is sent, as a weekly spot-check of what went out
At the start, when someone approves that the automation may run at all
Before the send: a named approver reviews the compiled report and its verification note
Nowhere, as long as the prompt instructs Claude to double-check all of its figures first
items.explanation: Gates belong where an error leaves your control. An external email is irreversible, so the named owner approves before sending.
distractors: Post-hoc checks find errors the client has already seen.
Approving the automation once doesn't review each week's content.
A self-check is a filter, not an accountable approval.

items.scenario: A Claude Code session ends with: 'Fixed the flaky test. I only modified files under tests/. All tests pass.' You are about to approve the PR.
items.question: What should your review be based on?
options: The agent's summary, since it ran the tests itself
The full diff, the changed-file list and the CI run, checked against the summary
A second prompt asking the agent to confirm it touched only files under tests/ and nothing else
The commit message, since it was generated from the actual changes
items.explanation: An agent's report is a claim. The evidence is the diff and CI. Review what it actually changed.
distractors: The summary can omit or misstate changes, such as an edited production timeout.
Asking again produces another claim, not evidence.
A generated commit message is also a summary, not the change itself.

items.scenario: A proposed workflow uses Claude to score 400 job applicants and automatically send rejection emails to the bottom 300.
items.question: What is the correct position?
options: Acceptable if the scoring prompt tells Claude to ignore protected characteristics and proxies for them
Acceptable if a human spot-checks ten rejections each week
Not acceptable: Claude may summarise or structure, but a human makes and records each decision
Acceptable if candidates are told in the job ad that AI is used
items.explanation: Hiring decisions are on the never-fully-automate list. They're consequential, bias-prone and regulated. Claude can assist. A human decides and records the reasons.
distractors: A prompt instruction doesn't remove bias or the need for human decision-making.
Sampling after the fact still leaves automated decisions about people.
Disclosure doesn't make automated rejection acceptable.

items.scenario: A generated dependency list contains a package whose registry entry shows no licence field, and the repository has no LICENSE file.
items.question: How should the audit classify it?
options: Allowed, since public code with no stated licence is effectively public domain
Allowed for internal tools only, since nobody will enforce it
Blocked until legal clears it, because no licence means no permission
Review only if it has fewer than 100 GitHub stars
items.explanation: Copyright applies by default. Without a licence you have no permission to use, modify or distribute the code.
distractors: Public visibility isn't a grant of rights. Public domain requires an explicit dedication.
The legal position doesn't depend on whether anyone enforces it.
Popularity has nothing to do with the licence.

items.scenario: A bid manager asks how to disclose AI use in a public-sector tender. Their draft adds 'AI may have been used in preparing this document' to every page.
items.question: What disclosure approach fits best?
options: Keep the blanket footer on every page, since more disclosure is always the safer choice in a bid
Remove it, since disclosure is never needed if a human reviewed the text
Follow the tender's and the organisation's rules, saying what AI did and what humans checked
Disclose only if the evaluators ask during clarification
items.explanation: Disclosure is driven by contract, policy or norm, and should be specific and proportional: what AI did and what was verified.
distractors: A vague blanket footer gives no useful information and may not meet a specific disclosure rule.
Human review doesn't cancel a disclosure requirement.
Rules usually require disclosure up front, not on request.

items.scenario: A client asks whether they will own the code your team writes with Claude. Your engagement lead replies: 'Yes. Anthropic's terms say outputs belong to the customer, so that settles it.'
items.question: What is wrong with this answer?
options: Nothing. Provider terms are the only document that governs who owns AI-generated output under any contract
It relies on one document; the client contract's IP clauses and employment terms also apply, so ask legal
It is wrong because AI-generated code can never be owned by anyone in any jurisdiction
It is wrong because only the individual developer can own code produced with their prompts
items.explanation: Provider terms cover you and the provider. The client contract (IP assignment, AI clauses) and employment terms cover the rest. Questions about the copyrightability of machine-generated material go to legal.
distractors: Provider terms don't govern the client relationship or employee assignment.
This overstates an unsettled area. The position varies and human authorship matters.
Employment and contract terms usually assign work product away from the individual.

items.scenario: You are designing scope limits for a scheduled agent that cleans up stale cloud resources in a client's staging account every night.
items.question: Which design best meets the agentic responsibilities in this module?
options: Admin credentials so it never fails, plus a summary email of what it reports deleting
Staging-scoped least-privilege credentials, a dry-run list a named owner approves, full logging and a stop procedure
Read-write credentials for every environment so it can also clean up production resources whenever someone asks it to
Least-privilege credentials and no logging, since staging resources are not important
items.explanation: The agent gets least privilege, a human gate before the irreversible step (deletion), an audit log, and a known way to stop it.
distractors: Admin credentials maximise the blast radius, and a self-reported summary isn't evidence.
Scope creep into production removes the boundary entirely.
Without logs you can't reconstruct or defend what the agent did.
